classification.difficultyReason: Complete the supplied unit-circle definition and directly identify the radian measure from an arc length of 2 and radius 1.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) completes the definition; part (b) applies it to an arc of length 2 on a unit circle.
questions.methodNote: No separate teaching pages were supplied. The embedded definition establishes arc length divided by radius.

classification.difficultyReason: Use half the circumference of a unit circle to obtain π radians, connect this with 180°, and double the relationship for a full turn; the sequence and diagrams supply the steps.

questions.mappingNote: The first two blanks precede the semicircle; its 180° conclusion follows the diagram. Part (b) doubles the semicircle relationship.
questions.methodNote: The source question itself connects unit-circle arc length with radian measure, then identifies a straight angle and a full turn.

classification.difficultyReason: Divide the established equivalence π radians = 180° by π or 180 to express one unit in the other measure.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess numerical conversion factors. The printed degree symbol in the answer-key denominator for F3(b) is removed because the prompt already supplies radians.
questions.methodNote: Divide the visible Fundamentals 2 equivalence 180° = π radians by π or 180 to obtain the conversion factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the same supplied conversion factor 180/π to each exact multiple of π and simplify; no new method or interpretation is required for angles exceeding one revolution.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve exact multiples of π use that conversion factor. Values greater than 2π retain their full degree measure.
questions.methodNote: The visible Fundamentals 2 and 3 establish π radians = 180° and the factor 180/π for conversion to degrees.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the stated degree-to-radian conversion in each part by multiplying by π/180 and simplifying; repeated angles add practice without requiring a new strategy.

questions.mappingNote: Every Q2 part directly assesses exact degree-to-radian conversion; four source columns retained in a–p order.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Authored solutions multiply the degree measure by π/180 to obtain radians.

classification.difficultyReason: Multiply each radian measure by 180/π, simplify exact multiples of π, and evaluate and round the remaining results to the nearest degree as instructed.

questions.mappingNote: The six radian inputs and nearest-degree instruction assess conversion in the reverse direction; three source columns retained.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Authored solutions multiply the radian measure by 180°/π, retain exact arithmetic and round only the final degree measure.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply π/180 to each degree measure, evaluate the result and round to one decimal place; the conversion direction and required precision are supplied.

questions.mappingNote: All six inputs assess degree-to-radian conversion with decimal rounding; three source columns retained. Exact key values remain visible as intermediate working.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Authored solutions multiply degrees by π/180, simplify exactly, then round to one decimal place as the student instruction requires.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the π/6 or π/3 reference angle, apply the quadrant signs to sine and cosine, and obtain tangent from their ratio. These are direct applications of taught exact-ratio methods; the repeated columns add no new reasoning demand.

questions.mappingNote: Eight angle columns assess exact ratios for multiples of π/6 and π/3. Each native child owns the three answers for its source column; the complete source table remains one editable table.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Authored solutions use exact special-angle ratios, reference angles and quadrant signs; tangent is sine divided by cosine.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply exact π/4 ratios and quadrant signs, read quadrantal values from unit-circle coordinates, and identify undefined tangent when cosine is zero. These are direct taught applications; repeated table entries add no new reasoning demand.

questions.mappingNote: Nine angle columns assess exact ratios for multiples of π/4, including quadrantal angles and undefined tangent. Each native child owns its source column's three answers.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence unavailable. Authored solutions use exact 45° ratios, quadrant signs, axis points on the unit circle and tangent as sine divided by cosine.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret each symbolic angle as a reflection or half-turn, use the supplied quadrant diagram to determine sine and cosine signs, and combine those signs for tangent. This requires routine linked use of angle symmetry and trigonometric ratios.

questions.mappingNote: Related-angle simplification in radians is closest to exact-ratios-radians in the supplied catalogue; no general related-angle skill was supplied.
questions.methodNote: Separate teaching pages were not supplied. The inspected question on PDF page 4 supplies quadrant signs. Solutions use circle reflections and a half-turn, with tangent expressed as sine divided by cosine.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret nested function notation, evaluate the inner function before the outer function, distinguish f(g(1)) from g(f(1)), and calculate trigonometric values in radians before rounding to two decimal places.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d respectively assess addition of function values and the compositions f(g(1)), h(g(0)) and g(f(1)). The closest supplied catalogue skill concerns trigonometric ratios in radians, although these tasks use calculator values rather than exact special-angle ratios.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate trigonometric functions in radians; evaluate the inner function first in a composition. Separate teaching evidence was not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the recalled radian definition by dividing each stated arc length by its radius, then compare the result with the claimed angle to decide true or false.

questions.mappingNote: Each statement directly tests the radian definition with its own stated arc length and radius.
questions.methodNote: Use radian measure as arc length divided by radius. The question itself supplies the defining unit-circle relationship; no separate teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect right-triangle sine and tangent ratios with unit-circle arc length, interpret how the three lengths compare for a small angle, and use the scaffolded comparison to infer both trigonometric ratios are approximately 1.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b establish perpendicular lengths; c establishes the highlighted arc length; d compares these for a small positive angle; e divides the approximate trigonometric equalities by nonzero theta. The supplied radian-definition skill is the closest catalogue match to this combined task.
questions.methodNote: Use right-triangle sine and tangent ratios, then unit-circle arc length, to motivate small-angle approximations in radians. Separate teaching pages and the full worked solutions referenced by the key were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the arc-length and sector-area formulas from a labelled sector; no calculation or rearrangement is required.

questions.mappingNote: The two formula-recall parts correspond individually to the labelled arc and sector.
questions.methodNote: Recall l = rθ and A = ½r²θ for an angle measured in radians. No separate teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify radians as the required unit and recall the degree-to-radian conversion factor within explicit completion scaffolds.

questions.mappingNote: Part a identifies the required unit; part b completes the general conversion statement. The supplied initial r is retained.
questions.methodNote: Use the angle-unit requirement for arc and sector formulae, then convert degrees to radians by multiplying by π/180. No separate teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the table headings to select l=rθ or its rearrangements, convert between degrees and radians, and express one calculated angle to the nearest minute. Each row supplies the necessary quantities directly.

questions.mappingNote: Each unlabelled source row has one answer-owning child. The native table preserves the four column meanings, every given and all eight empty response cells.
questions.methodNote: Use l = rθ, rearranging for θ or r where required, and use π radians = 180°. No separate teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the arc-length and sector-area formulas and substitute a supplied radius and radian angle; no conversion or rearrangement is needed.

questions.mappingNote: The source places the arc-length and sector-area parts in two columns; both use the shared radius and central angle.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the radius and radian angle into l = rθ and A = ½r²θ. No separate teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert the given central angle to radians, then directly substitute the radius and angle into the arc-length and sector-area formulas.

questions.mappingNote: The two response parts directly assess arc length and sector area for the same radius and central angle.
questions.methodNote: Convert degrees to radians, then use l=rθ and A=½r²θ. Teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the specified central angle for the corresponding arc and sector, convert it to radians, and substitute into the two familiar formulas.

questions.mappingNote: The chord identifies the bounding radii; the two requested quantities concern the corresponding 150° arc and sector.
questions.methodNote: Convert the central angle to radians and substitute into the arc-length and sector-area formulas. Teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange the arc-length formula to find the angle, then convert radians to degrees and the fractional degree to minutes with appropriate rounding.

questions.mappingNote: The source gives radius and arc length and requests the same central angle in two units.
questions.methodNote: Rearrange l=rθ to find the angle in radians, then convert to degrees and minutes. Teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that sector area determines the central angle, rearrange the sector-area formula, and use that angle in the arc-length formula.

questions.mappingNote: This connects the two formulas using a common radius and angle; no unverified shortcut is required.
questions.methodNote: Find the central angle from A=½r²θ, then use l=rθ. Teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Read the central angle from the diagram, convert it to radians, rearrange the sector-area formula for r² and select the positive square root.

questions.mappingNote: The diagram supplies the angle; the stem supplies the sector area.
questions.methodNote: Convert 60° to radians and rearrange the sector-area formula for a positive radius. Teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the wiper region as the outer sector minus the inner sector, use their common central angle and calculate the exact difference of their areas.

questions.mappingNote: The concentric arcs and radial boundaries identify an annular sector; the stem supplies both radii and its angle.
questions.methodNote: Calculate the difference between two sector areas with the same central angle. Teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange the sector-area formula separately for radius and angle, then recognise that the angle obtained in part (b) exceeds one full turn and cannot describe the stated ordinary sector.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) directly assesses radius; part (b) formally assesses angle but has incompatible numerical givens. Original student givens are retained pending resolution.
questions.methodNote: Rearrange A=½r²θ for the radius or angle and check that the angle is compatible with a single sector. Teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Subtract the removed angle from a full turn, convert the remaining angle to radians and use it in the sector-area and arc-length formulas.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) assesses the major-sector area remaining after removal; part (b) assesses the length of its major arc. Teaching-method confirmation remains unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. The solution converts the remaining angle to radians and uses the sector-area and arc-length formulas.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly requested cosine rule to the three given sides, obtain a radian angle, then use that angle to calculate the minor arc length.

questions.mappingNote: The three sides of triangle AOB determine its central angle; that angle determines the minor arc cut off by AB. No teaching pages were supplied to inspect.
questions.methodNote: The question explicitly requires the cosine rule followed by arc length. The worked solution follows that sequence and retains the unrounded angle for part (b).

classification.difficultyReason: Recover the central angle from arc length, calculate sector and triangle areas, then recognise and subtract those regions to obtain the shaded segment; the preceding parts scaffold the final connection.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a)–(d) combine arc length, sector area and minor-segment area, so arc-sector-segment-problems is the most advanced directly assessed supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was not supplied. Solutions use l = rθ, the sector-area formula, the sine area formula and sector-minus-triangle subtraction; these cannot be checked against this textbook's worked teaching.

classification.difficultyReason: Form arc-length and sector-area equations in two unknowns, eliminate the angle by division or substitution, and recover exact values; part (a) explicitly cues simultaneous equations before the parallel second task.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts combine the two sector formulas to recover radius and central angle; arc-sector-segment-problems is the closest supplied skill for this combined inverse problem.
questions.methodNote: The source question explicitly requires simultaneous equations in part (a). Both solutions form arc-length and sector-area equations and eliminate θ by division. No separate teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Use right-triangle cosine, recognise that the congruent tangent triangles double the calculated angle to give the minor central angle, then calculate the minor arc and subtract it from the circumference for the major arc.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed sequence combines tangent geometry, trigonometry and complementary arc lengths, making arc-sector-segment-problems the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. The stem supplies perpendicular radii and tangents; the solution uses right-triangle cosine, congruence to obtain the central angle, and l = rθ for minor and major arcs.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly requested cosine rule to the radius–chord triangle, then interpret road shortening as arc length minus chord length and retain the unrounded angle.

questions.mappingNote: The cosine-rule and arc-length sequence assesses a combined arc/chord application, so arc-sector-segment-problems is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Part (a) explicitly requires the cosine rule. Part (b) uses the resulting unrounded radian angle in l = rθ, then subtracts the chord length. No separate teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert the angle to radians, subtract concentric sector areas, and identify the complete annular-sector boundary as both arcs plus two radius differences.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) directly assesses the difference of two concentric sector areas. Part (b) directly assesses the complete boundary of the same annular sector. The source question and answer-book pages 45 and 46 were inspected; these answer pages do not establish the chapter's taught solution sequence.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. Independently solved by converting degrees to radians, subtracting sector areas using A = one half r squared theta, and adding both arc lengths and the two radial boundary segments using l = r theta.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the supplied hints to connect sector radius with cone slant height and sector arc with base circumference, then use Pythagoras and rearrange l=rθ. The parts explicitly scaffold these representation changes.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced assessed skill combines arc length with a sector folded into a cone.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. The printed hints establish the sector-radius/slant-height and sector-arc/base-circumference relationships; Pythagoras and l=rθ complete the solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret wheel rotation as linear travel using l=rθ, convert centimetres to metres, and convert distance per second into metres per minute.

questions.mappingNote: This is an application of arc length to linear motion and speed.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. Use l=rθ, convert centimetres to metres, divide by elapsed seconds and multiply by 60 for metres per minute.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the included-angle triangle and radian sector formulas, identify the segment as their area difference, and factor the result. Part (a) explicitly supplies the intermediate goals for the deduction.

questions.mappingNote: Deriving segment area directly assesses arc, sector and segment problems; sector area is a supporting skill.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages were supplied. The question itself scaffolds the derivation: write the triangle and sector areas, then subtract the triangle from the sector.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect unit-circle radii and the tangent ratio to two triangle areas, then translate strict containment of the triangle, sector and outer triangle into an inequality between functions. Earlier parts scaffold the area expressions, but the geometric comparison and its graphical interpretation require a non-trivial connection.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts share the unit-circle construction. Part (a) establishes the inner area; part (b) establishes the outer area; part (c) compares these with the sector; part (d) checks the same inequality graphically. Separate teaching-page evidence was not supplied.
questions.methodNote: The question explicitly directs comparison of the inner triangle, unit-circle sector and outer right triangle, followed by graphical verification. Solutions use the triangle area formula, the tangent ratio and the radian sector-area formula.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall standard circular-function terminology and the amplitude of sine and cosine, supported by initial-letter clues; no linked calculation is required.

questions.mappingNote: All seven printed parts assess basic properties of circular functions; graph-trig-functions is the closest supplied catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was not supplied. Complete terminology statements using periodicity, oscillation, extrema and amplitude.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify cotangent among the reciprocal functions and recognise that tangent asymptotes occur at odd multiples of π/2; the supplied forms and letter clues substantially scaffold both responses.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) assesses reciprocal-function terminology; part (b) directly assesses tangent asymptotes in radians, supporting graph-trig-radians.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was not supplied. Use reciprocal definitions and the zeros of cosine to explain tangent asymptotes.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the smallest positive repeat shifts of sine, cosine and tangent in radians, then transfer those same values to the period statement; no equation solving or representation change is required.

questions.mappingNote: The three periodic identities and concluding statement directly assess sine, cosine and tangent periods in radians.
questions.methodNote: Teaching evidence was not supplied. Identify the smallest positive repeat interval of each trigonometric function.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall quadrantal sine and cosine values, identify each supplied curve from its initial value and direction, and transfer the table values to graph labels. The table and supplied curves make this direct application.

questions.mappingNote: Graph recognition and annotation in radians are directly assessed; exact quadrantal ratios support the table.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. The question explicitly uses an exact-value table to identify and annotate graphs; solutions retain that progression.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine quadrantal tangent values and connect zeros with intercepts and undefined values with vertical asymptotes. The supplied branches and dashed asymptotes scaffold the graph interpretation.

questions.mappingNote: Tangent intercepts and vertical asymptotes in radians are directly assessed.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. The source explicitly connects a tangent value table to graph annotation.

classification.difficultyReason: Independently turn standard quadrantal values into sketches on the specified half-turn interval, placing the sine maximum, cosine intercept and tangent asymptote and choosing the correct direction for each tangent branch.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess basic trigonometric sketches in radians over [0,pi].
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Solutions use key quadrantal points and tangent asymptotes, consistent with Questions 1 and 2 on the inspected source page.

classification.difficultyReason: Extend standard trigonometric sketches to negative angles, locating quadrantal values and two tangent asymptotes and drawing the three increasing tangent branches on the specified interval.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess basic trigonometric sketches over a full turn containing negative angles.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were not supplied. Solutions use quadrantal points and tangent asymptotes, extending the table-and-graph progression visible in Questions 1 and 2 to negative angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch standard sine, cosine and tangent graphs across two periods using familiar exact zeros, extrema and asymptotes; the main demand is retaining the correct branches and endpoints over the extended domain.

questions.mappingNote: Each of the three printed functions is mapped to its own response part. Answer graphs were inspected on teacher pages 46 and 47.
questions.methodNote: Sketch from exact intercepts, turning points and vertical asymptotes. The supplied teaching pages are unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine first-quadrant ranges from standard trigonometric values and reciprocal definitions, distinguishing attained bounds from unbounded behaviour at undefined endpoints.

questions.mappingNote: The six printed functions retain their three-column, row-major arrangement. Undefined endpoint values are excluded when determining each range.
questions.methodNote: Read attainable y-values over the stated interval, using reciprocal definitions for cosecant, secant and cotangent. The supplied teaching pages are unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine positive and negative trigonometric values over the interval with reciprocal definitions to obtain disconnected cosecant and secant ranges, while recognising that tangent and cotangent attain every real value.

questions.mappingNote: The six printed functions retain their three-column, row-major arrangement. The answer key's redundant outer braces around the two union ranges are omitted in editable notation.
questions.methodNote: Read attainable y-values over the stated interval and use reciprocal definitions where required. The supplied teaching pages are unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch sine and its horizontal shift on shared axes, recognise the shifted curve as cosine, and express that relationship as an identity. The ordered drawing and comparison parts scaffold the connection.

questions.mappingNote: All four dependent parts remain in one question. Part (b) uses the drawing space allocated to part (a). The answer key's pink second series is mapped to standard red.
questions.methodNote: Compare a sine curve with its horizontal shift on the same axes, then recognise the cosine curve and state the identity. The activity itself supplies this graphical progression.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplify the quotient while retaining the original denominator restrictions, find all three excluded inputs, and represent them as holes on a constant graph. The explicit hint signals that cancellation alone is insufficient.

questions.mappingNote: The printed hint remains permanently visible inside the question prompt. The keyed graph is reconstructed as a solution-only mathematical visual.
questions.methodNote: Simplify the quotient while retaining the original denominator restrictions, then represent exclusions with open circles. The printed hint directs attention to these restrictions.

classification.difficultyReason: Critique the supplied algebra by distinguishing the domains of cotangent and reciprocal tangent, identify the two additional exclusions, and explain their graphical consequence despite agreement wherever both expressions are defined.

questions.mappingNote: The opening scenario and all supplied working belong to the parent prompt. The final unlabelled explanation request is the sole response leaf.
questions.methodNote: Compare the original domains of reciprocal tangent and cotangent. Bob's printed four-line manipulation is supplied question evidence and remains visible.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the standard interval and distinguish the periods of sine and cosine from tangent within supplied statements; no equation solving or domain filtering is required.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) recalls the standard interval and period for sine and cosine; part (b) contrasts the tangent period.
questions.methodNote: Complete the statements using the periods of sine, cosine and tangent. Separate teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise complementary-angle identities for sine and cosine and identify the corresponding cotangent expression; each response is a single directly recalled function.

questions.mappingNote: The compound-angle skill is the closest supplied catalogue entry for recognising functions of the argument pi over two minus x; this question assesses identities rather than equation solving.
questions.methodNote: Complete the complementary-angle identities in radians. Separate teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Read all intersections at the specified heights from supplied standard graphs, express their positions in radians and include both endpoints when they satisfy the equation.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (b) use the sine graph; part (c) uses the cosine graph; part (d) uses the tangent graph. The source question itself establishes the graphical method despite the absence of separate teaching pages.
questions.methodNote: The question explicitly supplies standard sine, cosine and tangent graphs to read every solution on the closed interval from minus two pi to two pi.

classification.difficultyReason: Count the supplied intersections, identify the two exact positive sine angles, and translate them by one period to obtain the negative-domain solutions.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts and the supplied graph form one question with the common equation and restricted domain.
questions.methodNote: Part (a) explicitly requires counting graph intersections. Part (b) uses exact reference angles and sine periodicity; teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Justify the supplied angles using the exact sine ratio, the two positive quadrants and repetition after 2π, explaining why these exhaust the stated domain.

questions.mappingNote: The four proposed values are permanent givens in this show-that task, not hidden response answers.
questions.methodNote: Exact reference angles, quadrant signs and the period 2pi establish all solutions; no teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply exact trigonometric ratios and quadrant signs within one revolution, including both endpoints when cosine equals 1.

questions.mappingNote: The common domain owns six distinct response parts, in the source three-column row order a,b,c then d,e,f.
questions.methodNote: Use exact unit-circle ratios and quadrant signs, retaining inclusive endpoints; teaching context was not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Find exact reference angles and appropriate quadrants, then use the different sine/cosine and tangent periods to select every solution across a domain containing negative angles.

questions.mappingNote: Four source parts share the symmetric domain and retain the four-column arrangement.
questions.methodNote: Use exact reference angles, quadrant signs and periodic repetitions into the negative part of the domain; teaching pages were not supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Select reciprocal or Pythagorean identities and factorisation across different equation forms, retain every valid factor, reject impossible ratios, and find all restricted-domain solutions. Parts (g) and (k) require several linked routine decisions, including reciprocal restrictions or multiple solution branches.

questions.mappingNote: One shared domain and rounding instruction governs twelve parts, retained in the source two-column row order a,b through k,l.
questions.methodNote: Use reciprocal and Pythagorean identities, factorisation, the zero-product rule, reference angles and inverse trigonometric functions. Preserve all valid factors and reject trigonometric values outside [-1,1]. No teaching pages were supplied to establish the textbook's preferred sequence.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply inverse trigonometric functions in radians and use quadrant symmetry to obtain the second solution. Part (b) first requires isolating cosine; all parts directly apply the taught procedure and round the results.
